title: 学会放手：为什么授权这么难
title_en: Why Delegating Is Harder Than It Looks
summary_zh: 让人升职的“什么都自己搞定”，恰恰是带团队时最该放下的习惯。这篇文章分析授权的两种常见失误，以及放手时最难的一关——情绪。读完你能用精确的英语谈论“交任务”和“放权”。
body: Nobody warns new team leaders that the skill which got them promoted is often the one they now have to give up. Being the person who fixes things quickly is a fine reputation for an individual; for a manager, it quietly turns into a bottleneck. Delegating sounds simple enough, yet most people who try it for the first time end up making one of two mistakes. Either they hand over the work but keep every decision, checking in so often that their colleague might as well be a pair of extra hands, or they disappear entirely and are then dismayed by the result. Neither counts as delegating in any useful sense. What separates genuine delegation from dumping is clarity about three things: what a good outcome looks like, how much freedom the other person has, and when you will check in. Unless you hand over the authority to decide as well as the task itself, you have not really delegated anything; you have simply created a slower way of doing it yourself. The harder part, though, is emotional. Watching someone take twice as long over a job you could finish in an afternoon is genuinely uncomfortable, and the temptation to step in can be overwhelming. Yet insisting on your own method misses the point. The aim is not to have the task done exactly as you would have done it, but to have it done well by someone who will be able to do it again without you. Some of the most effective leaders I have worked with treat a colleague's first attempt as an investment rather than a test. They expect it to be slower and slightly different, and they say so in advance, which takes the pressure off both sides. By the time the third attempt arrives on schedule and in good shape, the afternoon they sacrificed has been repaid many times over.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's central argument?
options: Managers should delegate only the tasks they dislike doing
Real delegation means passing on decisions too, and accepting a slower first result
Delegation works best when the manager reviews the work every day
New managers should keep fixing problems themselves to earn respect
questions.evidence: Unless you hand over the authority to decide as well as the task itself, you have not really delegated anything

questions.prompt: What does the writer mean by "a pair of extra hands"?
options: A colleague who simply follows instructions without making decisions
A colleague who is brought in to help for a short period
A colleague who is more skilled than the manager
A colleague who works on two projects at the same time
questions.evidence: checking in so often that their colleague might as well be a pair of extra hands

questions.prompt: Why does the writer say the sacrificed afternoon "has been repaid many times over"?
options: The colleague can now do the task alone, saving the leader time
The colleague worked an extra afternoon in return
The leader was paid for overtime
The task was cancelled in the end
questions.evidence: someone who will be able to do it again without you

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what must be clear for genuine delegation?
options: What a good outcome looks like, how much freedom the person has, and when you will check in
The deadline, the budget and the size of the team
Who will be blamed, who is paid and who decides
The method, the tools and the place of work
questions.evidence: what a good outcome looks like, how much freedom the other person has, and when you will check in

vocabulary.example: Approval from the finance team has become a bottleneck for every project.
She has a reputation for answering emails within the hour.
Team leads have the authority to approve small purchases.

vocabulary.meaning: 诱惑；忍不住想做的冲动
vocabulary.example: Resist the temptation to rewrite your colleague's slides.
Training a new hire properly is an investment, not a cost.

expressions.meaning: 简直就等于是；跟……没两样
expressions.note: 带一点讽刺，说某事实际上已经变成了别的东西：The meeting might as well be an email.

expressions.meaning: 从任何有意义的角度来说
expressions.note: 常用于否定句，严谨地否定一个说法：That isn't a plan in any useful sense.
可以是正面的“出手相助”，也可以像这里一样指“忍不住接管”。

expressions.meaning: 没抓住要点；搞错了重点
expressions.note: 评论别人的做法或论点时很常用：You're missing the point.
take the pressure off sb，说明某个做法让双方都轻松一些。
many times over 强调“好几倍”，常用于投入与回报：Her patience was repaid many times over.

knowledge.quote: Watching someone take twice as long over a job you could finish in an afternoon is genuinely uncomfortable
knowledge.explanation: 动名词短语 Watching someone take… 作主语，整个短语看作一件事，谓语用单数 is。注意 watch sb do sth 里 take 用原形。

knowledge.quote: Unless you hand over the authority to decide as well as the task itself, you have not really delegated anything
knowledge.explanation: unless = if… not，意为“除非”。用 unless 开头把必要条件放在最前面，语气比 if you don't… 更有判断力。

knowledge.quote: The aim is not to have the task done exactly as you would have done it, but to have it done well by someone who will be able to do it again without you.
knowledge.explanation: not to… but to… 两个不定式作表语，形成对比；have sth done 是使役结构，表示“让事情被（别人）完成”，正好贴合授权的主题。

speaking: 用 1 分钟讲讲你把一件事交给别人做（或别人交给你）的经历：交代清楚了吗？结果怎样？用上 step in 和 takes the pressure off。
writing: 用 200–250 词给第一次带小组的同学或新经理写一段建议：怎样“放手”才算真正授权。至少用一个 Unless…, … 句子和一个动名词作主语的句子。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 V-ing … is genuinely … 写一句话，描述一件明知应该做、却让你很难受的事。
task.model: Watching someone take twice as long over a job you could finish in an afternoon is genuinely uncomfortable

title: 最安静的同事，往往有最好的点子
title_en: The Quiet Colleague with the Best Ideas
summary_zh: 会上胜出的往往不是最好的点子，而是说得最早、最响的那个。作者认为不能把责任全推给“安静的人”，而应改变团队收集想法的方式。读完你能学会议论文中的让步、反驳与对比句式。
body: In most offices, the ideas that win are not necessarily the best ones but the ones voiced first and most confidently. This, I would argue, is one of the most expensive habits a team can have, because it quietly filters out people who prefer to think before they speak. Consider a typical planning meeting. Someone proposes a direction in the first few minutes, two others nod, and by the time Anil, who has been working out why the plan might fail, is ready to speak, the conversation has moved on. Raising the objection now would feel like reopening a settled question, so he says nothing, and the team discovers the flaw weeks later, when fixing it costs far more. It would be easy to conclude that quiet people simply need to speak up, and there is something to that. Nobody can read minds, and no workplace can be expected to chase every unspoken thought. Learning to interrupt politely is a genuinely useful skill, whatever your temperament. Yet putting the entire burden on the quieter person ignores how much the format itself shapes who contributes. Whereas open debate rewards speed, written input rewards reflection, and most teams rely almost entirely on the former. The remedies are not complicated. Circulating a short brief the day before allows people to arrive with considered views rather than first reactions. Opening with a few minutes of silent writing gives everyone the same starting line. And a chair who asks someone by name what they think sends a clear signal that contributions are wanted, not merely tolerated. Unless teams change how they gather ideas, they will keep mistaking volume for quality. The quiet colleague is rarely the problem to be solved; more often, they are the person who has already spotted it.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main claim?
options: Quiet employees should be trained to speak more confidently
Meetings should be replaced entirely by written reports
Teams should change how they collect ideas so that quieter people are heard
The first idea raised in a meeting is usually the strongest
questions.evidence: Yet putting the entire burden on the quieter person ignores how much the format itself shapes who contributes.

questions.prompt: Which point from the opposing view does the writer accept?
options: Quiet people rarely have ideas worth discussing
Learning to speak up is a valuable skill for anyone
Written input slows most teams down too much
A chair should avoid asking people by name
questions.evidence: Learning to interrupt politely is a genuinely useful skill, whatever your temperament.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest by saying the quiet colleague "has already spotted it"?
options: Teams should ignore late objections
Quiet colleagues should become managers
Quiet people cause most of a team's problems
Quiet people often notice flaws that others miss
questions.evidence: they are the person who has already spotted it

questions.prompt: What does "tolerated" mean in "wanted, not merely tolerated"?
options: allowed without really being welcomed
praised loudly
written down
paid for
questions.evidence: contributions are wanted, not merely tolerated

vocabulary.example: If nobody has an objection, we'll go ahead on Monday.
Her calm temperament makes her a good person to lead a crisis call.
The burden of organising the party always falls on the same person.
We discussed several remedies for the slow approval process.
Late arrivals are tolerated, but they are not encouraged.

expressions.note: 议论文和讨论中先部分认同对方的经典说法，后面通常接 Yet / But 转折。
既可以指“大声点”，也常指“说出自己的意见”：Don't be afraid to speak up.
settled 表示“已经决定了的”，reopen a settled question 就是“翻旧账、重新讨论”。
move on 也可以指“放下过去、继续前进”，这里指对话已进入下一个话题。
比喻机会平等，中英文意象相同，书面和口语都可以用。

expressions.meaning: 把“声音大”误当成“质量好”
expressions.note: mistake A for B 指把 A 误认为 B；volume 一语双关，既是“音量”也是“数量”。

knowledge.quote: Circulating a short brief the day before allows people to arrive with considered views rather than first reactions.
knowledge.explanation: 动名词短语 Circulating a short brief the day before 作主语，谓语用单数 allows。用动名词作主语提建议，比 You should circulate… 更客观、更像论证。

knowledge.quote: Whereas open debate rewards speed, written input rewards reflection
knowledge.explanation: Whereas 引导对比状语从句，把两种做法并排比较，结构平行（A rewards X, B rewards Y），比 but 更正式、更书面。

knowledge.quote: Unless teams change how they gather ideas, they will keep mistaking volume for quality.
knowledge.explanation: Unless + 一般现在时，主句 will + 动词原形：除非条件发生，否则后果会一直持续。用在结论段，给读者一个明确的“必须改变”的信号。

speaking: 用 1 分钟回答：在你参加过的讨论里，最后被采纳的通常是“最好的”想法，还是“最先说出来”的想法？举一个例子，并用上 there is something to that 和 Whereas…, …。
writing: 用 220–260 词写一篇观点文章：团队讨论应该怎样让不爱发言的人也被听见。要有明确论点、一个让步（… and there is something to that），以及一个以 Unless 开头的结论句。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 Whereas A rewards …, B rewards … 对比两种做法分别“奖励”了什么样的人或能力。
task.model: Whereas open debate rewards speed, written input rewards reflection

title: 书评：《午饭前只做一件事》
summary_zh: 一本虚构的效率书，核心方法简单到能写在便利贴上。书评人既肯定它对拖延小把戏的精准描写，也指出它默认人人都能掌控早晨的局限。读完你能学会写一篇有褒有贬的书评。
body: Productivity books tend to make the same promise: adopt the system and you will finally feel in control. The appeal of Margit Holloway's "One Thing Before Lunch" is that it promises considerably less. Its central idea fits on a sticky note: choose the single task that would make today feel worthwhile, and do it before you open your inbox. Everything else in the book is an attempt to explain why something so obvious is so rarely done. Holloway is at her best when describing the small evasions we all recognise: tidying a desk to avoid writing a report, answering easy messages to feel busy, or scheduling a meeting about a decision we are afraid to make. Reading these chapters is mildly uncomfortable, in the way that hearing a recording of your own voice is uncomfortable. Where the book is weaker is in its assumption that every reader controls their own morning. Unless your first hour genuinely belongs to you, much of the advice reads as if it were written for someone else. Holloway acknowledges this in a brief final chapter, but her suggestions for shift workers and parents of small children feel like an afterthought. To be fair, she never claims to have invented anything. Although the method itself is hardly new, the tone is refreshingly free of the combative language, all "crushing" goals and "winning" mornings, that dominates the genre. She writes like a sensible friend rather than a drill sergeant, and the book is short enough to finish in two evenings. I did exactly that and, somewhat to my own surprise, have been doing my one thing before lunch ever since. Whether the habit survives a truly chaotic week is another question. Still, for a book of this kind, changing anything at all is a fairly high bar, and this one clears it.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's overall judgement of the book?
options: It is highly original and makes other productivity books unnecessary
It is useful and honest, although its advice does not suit every reader
It is too long and mostly repeats ideas from other books
It is written mainly for shift workers and busy parents
questions.evidence: for a book of this kind, changing anything at all is a fairly high bar, and this one clears it

questions.prompt: Why does the reviewer compare reading some chapters to hearing a recording of your own voice?
options: The chapters are written in a very personal, spoken style
The chapters show readers habits they recognise in themselves but would rather not see
The chapters were first published as an audio programme
The chapters repeat the same point too many times
questions.evidence: Holloway is at her best when describing the small evasions we all recognise

questions.prompt: What does "evasions" mean in "the small evasions we all recognise"?
options: small mistakes in writing
ways of saving money
short breaks for coffee
ways of avoiding something we should do
questions.evidence: the small evasions we all recognise

questions.prompt: What is the central idea of the book?
options: Wake up an hour earlier
Answer every email before lunch
Choose the one task that would make today worthwhile and do it before opening your inbox
Plan every hour of the week in advance
questions.evidence: choose the single task that would make today feel worthwhile, and do it before you open your inbox

vocabulary.example: His long explanations were really just polite evasions.
The plan rests on the assumption that everyone has a laptop.
The report acknowledges that the timeline was too ambitious.

vocabulary.meaning: 事后补上的东西；次要的附加
vocabulary.example: The vegetarian option on the menu felt like an afterthought.
The new manager is refreshingly honest about what she doesn't know.

expressions.note: 形容一个想法极其简单，带点幽默；类似说法还有 fits on the back of an envelope。
评论作者、演员、球员时很常用：The film is at its best in the quiet scenes.
书评、产品评论里批评某部分“不用心”的地道说法。
批评之后替对方说句好话，让评价显得平衡，口语书面都很常用。
to my surprise 的加强版，somewhat 让语气更克制、更书面。
bar 指标准、门槛；clear the bar 就是“达到标准”，常见于评价和招聘语境。

knowledge.quote: Reading these chapters is mildly uncomfortable, in the way that hearing a recording of your own voice is uncomfortable.
knowledge.explanation: 两个动名词短语 Reading these chapters 和 hearing a recording… 分别作主语，结构平行，用来类比两种相似的感受。动名词作主语时谓语用单数。

knowledge.quote: To be fair, she never claims to have invented anything.
knowledge.explanation: To be fair 是固定的不定式插入语；claims to have invented 用完成式不定式，表示“声称已经发明了”，动作发生在 claims 之前。

knowledge.quote: Although the method itself is hardly new, the tone is refreshingly free of the combative language
knowledge.explanation: Although 引导让步状语从句，先承认缺点（方法不新），再在主句里给出优点。书评中先抑后扬，评价显得更可信。

speaking: 用 1 分钟评价一本你读过的书、一门课或一个 App：先说它最出彩的地方，再说一个不足，最后给出总体评价。用上 To be fair 和 is at its best when…。
writing: 用 200–250 词写一篇书评或 App 测评：包括核心观点、最打动你的地方、一个明显的局限，以及你的最终评价。至少用一个 Although 句和一个动名词作主语的句子。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 V-ing … is …, in the way that V-ing … is … 写一句类比，描述一种复杂的感受。
task.model: Reading these chapters is mildly uncomfortable, in the way that hearing a recording of your own voice is uncomfortable.

title: 如何得体地提出谈薪
title_en: How to Ask for a Conversation About Pay
summary_zh: 提出谈薪让几乎所有人都紧张。这篇指南只讲沟通：怎样单独约时间、先讲贡献而不是抱怨，以及被拒绝时怎样把“现在不行”变成一个时间表。读完你能得体地开启这场对话。
body: Asking to talk about pay makes almost everyone uneasy, partly because it seems to mix two things we prefer to keep apart: our relationship with a manager and our sense of what our work is worth. The good news is that the request itself does not need to be dramatic. Treating it as a normal professional conversation, rather than a confrontation, is half the work. Start by asking for the meeting separately, instead of raising the subject at the end of an unrelated catch-up. A short message such as "I'd like to set aside some time to talk about my role and pay; would sometime next week suit you?" signals that you are serious without sounding like an ultimatum. It also gives your manager the chance to prepare, which works in your favour, since few people respond well to being ambushed. Before the meeting, write down what has changed since your role was last discussed: responsibilities you have taken on, problems you have solved, colleagues you now support. Unless your manager can see that picture clearly, they will struggle to make the case on your behalf, and in many organisations the decision is not theirs alone. In the conversation itself, lead with your contribution rather than your frustration. Saying "I've taken on the supplier contracts and the new starters' training, and I'd like us to look at whether my pay reflects that" is far easier to hear than a list of grievances. Then stop talking and listen. If the answer is "not now", ask what would need to happen for it to become "yes", and agree on when you will revisit it. That single question turns a closed door into a timetable. Finally, follow up in writing with a brief, friendly summary of what you both agreed. Doing so protects everyone from vague memories, and it shows that you intend to keep the conversation going.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the guide?
options: It is better to raise the subject casually at the end of another meeting
Asking about pay works best as a calm, prepared, professional conversation
Pay should only ever be discussed during a formal annual review
You should keep talking until your manager agrees to your request
questions.evidence: Treating it as a normal professional conversation, rather than a confrontation, is half the work.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer suggest asking for the meeting in advance?
options: It gives the manager time to prepare, which helps you
It lets you avoid discussing the subject face to face
It means the decision can be made before the meeting
It shows the manager that you are ready to leave
questions.evidence: It also gives your manager the chance to prepare, which works in your favour

questions.prompt: Why does asking "what would need to happen" turn "a closed door into a timetable"?
options: It ends the conversation quickly
It forces the manager to say yes
It shows the manager that you are angry
It changes a refusal into a plan with steps and a date
questions.evidence: That single question turns a closed door into a timetable.

questions.prompt: What does "ambushed" mean in "few people respond well to being ambushed"?
options: surprised by something without warning
thanked in public
promoted
ignored
questions.evidence: few people respond well to being ambushed

vocabulary.example: I wanted a quiet chat, not a confrontation in front of the team.
Giving your team an ultimatum rarely improves the work.

vocabulary.meaning: 被突然袭击；被打个措手不及
vocabulary.example: He felt ambushed when the topic came up without any warning.
The meeting turned into a long list of old grievances.
Let's revisit the budget once the first stage is finished.

expressions.note: 约人谈正事时的礼貌说法，比 have a chat 正式，显得你重视这次谈话。
work in sb's favour 指情况朝着对某人有利的方向发展。

expressions.text: make the case on your behalf
expressions.meaning: 替你争取；代表你去说明理由
expressions.note: make the case 指摆出理由说服别人；on sb's behalf 是“代表某人”。
lead with sth 指“以……开头”，沟通中先说什么往往决定了对方怎么听。

expressions.text: turns a closed door into a timetable
expressions.note: 比喻把拒绝变成可以跟进的计划，是很有画面感的书面表达。
表示事情还没结束、双方会继续沟通，职场和社交场合都适用。

knowledge.quote: Treating it as a normal professional conversation, rather than a confrontation, is half the work.
knowledge.explanation: 动名词短语 Treating it as… 作主语，谓语用单数 is；中间插入 rather than a confrontation 作对比。用动名词作主语，能把一种“做法”当成话题来评价。

knowledge.quote: Unless your manager can see that picture clearly, they will struggle to make the case on your behalf
knowledge.explanation: Unless = if… not：除非经理能看清楚你的变化，否则很难替你争取。用 unless 强调准备工作是必要条件。

knowledge.quote: It also gives your manager the chance to prepare, which works in your favour, since few people respond well to being ambushed.
knowledge.explanation: since 引导原因状语从句，解释前面的判断为什么成立；which 引导的非限制性定语从句指代前面整件事。注意 respond well to being ambushed 中 to 后接动名词的被动式。

speaking: 假设你想和负责人谈谈你的工作量或职责变化，用 1 分钟练习开场：先约时间，再用一两句话说明你做了哪些新工作。用上 set aside some time 和 lead with…。
writing: 用 150–200 词写一封邮件，约你的上级（或导师、社团负责人）谈谈你的角色和待遇：语气礼貌、目的清楚，不提具体数字，并说明你希望谈哪些方面。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 V-ing …, rather than …, is half the work 写一句话，说明做好一件难事的关键心态。
task.model: Treating it as a normal professional conversation, rather than a confrontation, is half the work.
